teenWords.meaning: To represent something as being larger or greater than it really is.

teenWords.meaning: Present, appearing, or found everywhere simultaneously.

teenWords.meaning: Characterized by vulgar or pretentious display; designed to impress.

teenWords.meaning: A revival of or renewed interest in arts, literature, science, or culture.
teenWords.tip: Single N, double S, ends in -ANCE: RE-NAI-SS-ANCE!
teenWords.sentence: The discovery of clean fusion energy sparked a global industrial renaissance.

teenWords.meaning: Supreme power, authority, or independent self-governance of a state.
teenWords.tip: Look for 'REIGN' inside: SOV-E-REIGN-TY!
teenWords.sentence: The island nation defended its maritime sovereignty before the international tribunal.

teenWords.meaning: Temporarily not awake or aware of one's surroundings; done without deliberate thought.
teenWords.tip: Contains 'SC' for /s/ and 'C' for /sh/: UN-CON-SC-I-OUS!
teenWords.sentence: The hockey player remained unconscious for a few moments after the hard collision.

teenWords.root: Latin 'vaccinus' (of cows, from vacca cow, where cowpox was studied)
teenWords.meaning: To administer an antigenic preparation to stimulate the immune system against a disease.
teenWords.tip: Double C: V-A-CC-I-N-A-T-E!
teenWords.sentence: Public health clinics organized weekend clinics to vaccinate incoming freshmen.

teenWords.root: Medieval Latin 'collateralis' (con- together + lateralis of the side)
teenWords.meaning: Something pledged as security for repayment of a loan; accompanying as secondary.
teenWords.tip: Double L in the middle: COL-LAT-ER-AL!
teenWords.sentence: Commercial borrowers frequently offer real estate holdings as collateral.

teenWords.meaning: To irritate, annoy, or infuriate someone to an intense degree.
teenWords.tip: EX + ASPER (rough) + ATE -- no extra 's' or 'c' after ex!
teenWords.sentence: Long airport security delays never failed to exasperate tired travelers.

teenWords.root: Latin 'inoculare' (in- into + oculus eye or plant bud)
teenWords.meaning: To introduce an antigenic substance or microorganism into an organism or culture medium.
teenWords.tip: Only ONE 'N' and ONE 'C': IN-OC-U-LATE (frequently misspelled with double c)!
teenWords.sentence: Botanists inoculate seedling roots with mycorrhizal fungi to enhance nutrient uptake.

teenWords.meaning: A thing that is required as a prior condition for something else to happen or exist.
teenWords.tip: PRE + REQUISITE (ends in -ITE, not -ate)!
teenWords.sentence: Passing differential calculus is a strict prerequisite for quantum mechanics.

teenWords.meaning: Fine nuances, delicate distinctions, or elusive details.
teenWords.tip: Silent 'B' in SUB-TLE-TIES!
teenWords.sentence: The literary translator spent months capturing the cultural subtleties of the prose.

teenWords.meaning: Cruel, unreasonable, or arbitrary use of power or governing authority.
teenWords.tip: Single R, double N: TY-RA-NN-Y!
teenWords.sentence: The revolutionaries drafted a constitution specifically designed to thwart executive tyranny.

teenWords.meaning: Of the same kind; alike in structure, quality, or constituent elements throughout.
teenWords.tip: HOMO + GENE + OUS (keep the 'E' after gene)!
teenWords.sentence: The alloy was stirred at high temperatures to ensure a completely homogeneous mixture.

teenWords.meaning: Absolutely necessary, essential, or impossible to manage without.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ABLE (not -ible): IN-DIS-PENS-ABLE!
teenWords.sentence: A reliable spectrophotometer is an indispensable instrument in biochemistry.

teenWords.meaning: Something placed out of its historical or chronological time period.
teenWords.tip: ANA + CHRON (time) + ISM -- 'CH' makes the /k/ sound!
teenWords.sentence: A digital wristwatch visible on an ancient Roman soldier is a glaring cinematic anachronism.

teenWords.meaning: A harsh, discordant, jarring mixture of sounds or noises.
teenWords.tip: CAC-O-PHON-Y ('PH' for /f/ sound, ending in -Y)!
teenWords.sentence: A cacophony of blaring horns and drilling jackhammers echoed down Fifth Avenue.

teenWords.meaning: Showing extreme care and great attention to precise details.
teenWords.tip: ME-TIC-U-LOUS (single T, ends in -LOUS)!
teenWords.sentence: Through meticulous archival research, she uncovered previously lost correspondence.

teenWords.meaning: Having a harmful, destructive effect, especially in a gradual or insidious manner.
teenWords.tip: PER-NI-CIOUS ('C' produces the /sh/ sound before -ious)!
teenWords.sentence: Counterfeit currency can exert a pernicious influence on economic stability.

teenWords.root: Latin 'surrepticius' (sub- under + rapere to seize secretly)
teenWords.meaning: Kept secret or done stealthily, especially because it would meet with disapproval.
teenWords.tip: Double R, double T: SUR-REP-TI-TIOUS!
teenWords.sentence: The undercover agent cast a surreptitious glance toward the exit before transmitting data.

teenWords.root: Greek 'esoterikos' (esotero inner, belonging to an inner circle)
teenWords.meaning: Intended for or understood by only an enlightened or initiated few.
teenWords.tip: E-SO-TER-IC (single S and single T)!
teenWords.sentence: Theoretical physics seminars often delve into highly esoteric mathematical proofs.

teenWords.root: Greek 'Lakonikos' (from Laconia/Sparta, famous for concise, terse speech)
teenWords.meaning: Using very few words in speech or writing; concise to the point of seeming blunt.
teenWords.tip: LA-CON-IC (spelled with 'C's, no 'k')!
teenWords.sentence: The mountain guide answered our anxious questions with a laconic nod and two words: 'Follow me.'

teenWords.root: Latin 'obsequium' (compliance, from obsequi to follow obediently)
teenWords.meaning: Obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree; sycophantic.
teenWords.tip: OB-SEQ-UI-OUS (look for Q-U-I in the middle)!
teenWords.sentence: Courtiers displayed obsequious deference whenever the emperor entered the banquet hall.

teenWords.meaning: Wanting or devouring immense quantities of food, or eagerly consuming knowledge.
teenWords.tip: VOR-A-CIOUS (starts with VOR- like carnivore, distinct from veracious)!
teenWords.sentence: As a young student, she was a voracious reader who finished three books each weekend.

teenWords.root: Latin 'recalcitrare' (re- back + calcitrare to kick, from calx heel)
teenWords.meaning: Obstinately uncooperative and defiant toward authority, rules, or instruction.
teenWords.tip: RE-CAL-CI-TRANT ('C' before 'I' sounds like /s/)!
teenWords.sentence: The recalcitrant committee refused to approve the revised budget despite repeated pleas.

teenWords.meaning: Open to more than one interpretation; intentionally ambiguous or misleading.
teenWords.tip: EQUI (equal) + VOC (voice) + AL (saying two different things equally)!
teenWords.sentence: The politician gave an equivocal response when pressed on whether taxes would rise.

teenWords.meaning: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; having excessively demanding standards.
teenWords.tip: FAS-TID-I-OUS (single S, ends in -IOUS)!
teenWords.sentence: The museum curator was fastidious about maintaining precise humidity in the gallery.

teenWords.meaning: Exceeding what is necessary, required, or sufficient; redundant.
teenWords.tip: SUPER + FLU (flow) + OUS (overflowing beyond what is needed)!
teenWords.sentence: Word processors easily flag superfluous adjectives that weaken academic arguments.

teenWords.root: Latin 'gregarius' (belonging to a flock, from grex/gregis herd)
teenWords.meaning: Fond of company and highly sociable; living in organized flocks, packs, or herds.
teenWords.tip: GREG (herd/flock) + AR-IOUS!
teenWords.sentence: Dolphins are gregarious marine mammals that hunt and travel in coordinated pods.

teenWords.root: Spanish 'los intransigentes' via French from Latin 'in-' (not) + 'transigere' (to compromise)
teenWords.meaning: Unwilling or refusing to alter one's stance or come to an agreement; unyielding.
teenWords.tip: IN-TRAN-SI-GENT (ends in -GENT, not -jant)!
teenWords.sentence: Negotiations collapsed because both negotiating teams adopted intransigent positions.

teenWords.meaning: To make something bad, painful, or unsatisfactory significantly better; improve.
teenWords.tip: Contains 'MELIOR' (Latin for better): A-MEL-I-OR-ATE!
teenWords.sentence: Urban planting initiatives help ameliorate the stifling heat island effect in city centers.

teenWords.root: Latin 'belliger' (bellum war + gerere to wage or carry on)
teenWords.meaning: Hostile, aggressive, and combat-ready; engaged in warfare.
teenWords.tip: Double L in the middle: BEL-LIG-ER-ENT!
teenWords.sentence: The diplomat condemned the belligerent rhetoric broadcast by the rogue military regime.

teenWords.root: Italian 'capriccio' (fright or sudden shiver like a bounding goat, capra)
teenWords.meaning: Given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood, attitude, or behavior; erratic.
teenWords.tip: CAP-RI-CIOUS ('C-I' for the /sh/ sound before -OUS)!
teenWords.sentence: Mountain weather can be notoriously capricious, turning from bright sunshine to hail in minutes.

teenWords.meaning: To make someone feeble, infirm, or drastically weaker.
teenWords.tip: DE-BIL-I-TATE (single L, ends in -ATE)!
teenWords.sentence: Untreated Lyme disease can debilitate athletes with chronic joint inflammation.

teenWords.root: Latin 'enervare' (e- out of + nervus sinew, nerve, or vigor)
teenWords.meaning: To drain someone of physical, mental, or moral energy; weaken or deplete.
teenWords.tip: E-NER-VATE -- contrary to intuition, it means to exhaust, NOT to energize!
teenWords.sentence: Intense tropical humidity combined with a steep mountain ascent served to enervate the hikers.

teenWords.meaning: Tending to talk a great deal; extremely communicative or verbose.
teenWords.tip: LO-QUA-CIOUS (look for QUA in the middle and -CIOUS at the end)!
teenWords.sentence: The loquacious tour guide regaled passengers with centuries of local folklore.

teenWords.meaning: Well-meaning, kindly, and dedicated to philanthropic deeds rather than profit.
teenWords.tip: BENE (good) + VOL (wish) + ENT (wishing well for others)!
teenWords.sentence: A benevolent patron funded scholarships for dozens of underprivileged STEM students.

teenWords.meaning: Brisk and cheerful readiness; lively promptness in action.
teenWords.tip: A-LAC-RI-TY (single L, single C, ends in -ITY)!
teenWords.sentence: When offered an internship at NASA, the young engineer accepted with unbounded alacrity.

teenWords.root: Greek 'pragmatikos' (relating to deed, action, or fact, from prassein to do)
teenWords.meaning: Dealing with challenges realistically and sensibly based on practical outcomes.
teenWords.tip: PRAG-MAT-IC (related to praxis and pragmatism)!
teenWords.sentence: Rather than waiting for ideal legislation, the mayor adopted a pragmatic pilot program.

teenWords.root: Latin 'aberrare' (ab- away from + errare to wander or stray)
teenWords.meaning: A departure from what is normal, usual, or standard, typically an unwelcome variation.
teenWords.tip: Single B, double R: AB-ERR-ATION (wandering away)!
teenWords.sentence: The unexpected spike in baseline temperature readings was dismissed as an instrumental aberration.

teenWords.meaning: The dramatic treatment of light and shadow in painting, drawing, or cinematography.
teenWords.tip: CHI-A-RO-SCU-RO (Italian CHI- sounds like /k/)!
teenWords.sentence: Caravaggio mastered the technique of chiaroscuro to imbue biblical portraits with intense realism.

teenWords.meaning: An expert judge in matters of fine art, cuisine, music, or refined taste.
teenWords.tip: Double N, OIS, double S, and ends in French -EUR: CON-NOIS-SEUR!
teenWords.sentence: As a trained connoisseur of classical violins, she could identify a Stradivarius by tone alone.

teenWords.meaning: To remove all moisture from something; cause to become completely dried out.
teenWords.tip: Single S, double C: DE-SIC-CATE (often confused with double s)!
teenWords.sentence: Arid desert winds will rapidly desiccate exposed biological specimens.

teenWords.meaning: Light, delicate, and translucent (especially describing fine fabrics or morning mists).
teenWords.tip: DIA + PHAN (show) + OUS -- uses 'PH' for the /f/ sound!
teenWords.sentence: Sunlight filtered gently through the diaphanous silk curtains in the atrium.

teenWords.root: Latin 'efflorescere' (ex- out + florere to blossom or flower)
teenWords.meaning: The state or period of blossoming; the migration of salt crystals to a masonry surface.
teenWords.tip: Double F, SC in the middle, ends in -ENCE: EF-FLO-RE-SC-ENCE!
teenWords.sentence: White mineral efflorescence appeared across the aged brick foundation after the rainy season.

teenWords.meaning: Pleasure or satisfaction derived by someone from another person's misfortune.
teenWords.tip: Starts with German SCH-, contains EU: SCHA-DEN-FREU-DE!
teenWords.sentence: Spectators felt an unworthy prickle of schadenfreude when the arrogant champion slipped on the turn.

teenWords.root: Latin 'sesquipedalis' (sesqui- one and a half + pedalis foot-long)
teenWords.meaning: Characterized by long words; given to using polysyllabic or foot-and-a-half-long vocabulary.
teenWords.tip: SES-QUI-PE-DAL-I-AN (literally foot-and-a-half long)!
teenWords.sentence: The satirical columnist mocked the professor's sesquipedalian prose style.

teenWords.root: Greek 'Terpsikhore' (the Muse of choral dance, from terpein to delight + khoros dance)
teenWords.meaning: Relating to dance, ballet, or rhythmic theatrical choreography.
teenWords.tip: TERP-SI-CHO-RE-AN ('CH' produces the /k/ sound)!
teenWords.sentence: The Broadway prodigy amazed talent scouts with her extraordinary terpsichorean prowess.

teenWords.meaning: Relating to, supported by, or dependent upon charitable donations and alms.
teenWords.tip: E-LEE-MOS-Y-NARY (double E, with S-Y)!
teenWords.sentence: The hospice foundation operates strictly on an eleemosynary endowment fund.

teenWords.root: Latin 'tintinnabulum' (a small bell, from tintinnare to jingle)
teenWords.meaning: A ringing, pealing, or jingling sound, particularly of bells.
teenWords.tip: Double N in the middle: TIN-TIN-NAB-U-LA-TION (immortalized by Edgar Allan Poe)!
teenWords.sentence: The crisp winter morning echoed with the tintinnabulation of distant cathedral chimes.

teenWords.meaning: A change of circumstance or fortune, typically one that is unwelcome or unpredictable.
teenWords.tip: VI-CIS-SI-TUDE (single C, double S)!
teenWords.sentence: Seasoned entrepreneurs learn to navigate every economic vicissitude with poise.

teenWords.meaning: Having keen mental insight and understanding; shrewdly perceptive.
teenWords.tip: PER-SPI-CA-CIOUS ('C-I' before -OUS, distinct from perspicuous)!
teenWords.sentence: The perspicacious detective noticed subtle timeline discrepancies in the suspect's testimony.

teenWords.meaning: The defining spirit, intellectual outlook, or cultural mood of a particular era.
teenWords.tip: ZEIT (time) + GEIST (spirit): Z-E-I-T-G-E-I-S-T!
teenWords.sentence: The protest anthems of the late 1960s captured the restless zeitgeist of a generation.

teenWords.root: Latin 'inchoare' (to begin, start a web upon a loom)
teenWords.meaning: Just begun, in an initial stage, and not yet clearly formed or organized; rudimentary.
teenWords.tip: IN-CHO-ATE ('CH' pronounced /k/)!
teenWords.sentence: Her political philosophy was still inchoate during her freshman year of university.

teenWords.meaning: Excessive and often uncontrollable talkativeness or rambling wordiness.
teenWords.tip: LOGO + RRHEA (double R followed by H, like diarrhea)!
teenWords.sentence: Nervousness brought on an acute bout of logorrhea during his first televised debate.

teenWords.meaning: The scientific branch of entomology devoted to the study of ants.
teenWords.tip: Starts with MYR- (like myrrh): MYR-ME-COL-O-GY!
teenWords.sentence: Dr. E. O. Wilson made landmark evolutionary discoveries in the field of myrmecology.

teenWords.root: Greek 'panakes' (pan- all + akos cure or remedy)
teenWords.meaning: A remedy or solution claimed to solve all problems, ills, or diseases.
teenWords.tip: PAN (all) + ACEA: P-A-N-A-C-E-A!
teenWords.sentence: Economists caution that deregulation is never an instant panacea for structural inflation.

teenWords.meaning: The state of being close or proximate in space, time, or relationship.
teenWords.tip: PRO-PIN-QUI-TY (contains P-I-N-Q-U-I)!
teenWords.sentence: Daily physical propinquity in the cramped research submarine forged lifelong bonds.

teenWords.meaning: Attractive and strikingly impressive through glowing radiance, color, or elegance.
teenWords.tip: RE-SPLEN-DENT (ends in -ENT, not -ant)!
teenWords.sentence: The peacock unfurled its resplendent tail feathers beneath the botanical canopy.

teenWords.root: Latin 'subterfugere' (subter beneath or secretly + fugere to flee)
teenWords.meaning: Deceit or artifice used to evade a rule, escape a consequence, or conceal true motives.
teenWords.tip: SUB-TER-FUGE (ends in -UGE)!
teenWords.sentence: The smugglers relied on elaborate diplomatic subterfuge to bypass customs inspections.

teenWords.meaning: The state of being away or not present.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ence, not -ense: think 'absent' plus '-ce'.
teenWords.sentence: Her absence from the meeting was noticed by everyone.

teenWords.meaning: Satisfactory; good enough to be received or approved.
teenWords.tip: It is -able, not -ible: accept + able.
teenWords.sentence: A grade of B was acceptable to Maya, though she had hoped for an A.

teenWords.root: Latin 'accidens' (a happening) from ad- + cadere (to fall)
teenWords.meaning: By chance; without intending to.
teenWords.tip: Keep the full '-ally': accidental + ly, never 'accidently'.
teenWords.sentence: He accidentally deleted the only copy of his essay.

teenWords.root: Old French 'achever' (to bring to a head)
teenWords.meaning: To successfully reach a goal through effort.
teenWords.tip: I before E in 'achieve' — it follows the classic rule.
teenWords.sentence: With steady practice, she achieved her goal of running a marathon.

teenWords.meaning: To gain or obtain something.
teenWords.tip: Starts with ACQ — the C is easy to forget: think 'acquisition'.
teenWords.sentence: The museum hopes to acquire the rare painting next year.

teenWords.root: Old French 'adresser' (to direct) from Latin ad- + directus
teenWords.meaning: The details of where someone lives or where mail is sent; also, to speak formally to.
teenWords.tip: Double D and double S: a-DD-re-SS.
teenWords.sentence: Please write your home address at the top of the form.

teenWords.meaning: Ready to attack or confront; forceful.
teenWords.tip: Two G's and two S's: a-GG-re-SS-ive.
teenWords.sentence: The aggressive dog barked at every stranger who passed.

teenWords.root: Latin 'allegare' (to send with a message, cite)
teenWords.meaning: Claimed to have happened, though not yet proven.
teenWords.tip: Double L, then -eged: a-LL-eged.
teenWords.sentence: The alleged thief was caught on camera near the shop.

teenWords.meaning: A person who does an activity for pleasure, not for pay.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -eur like other French borrowings: amat-EUR.
teenWords.sentence: Though only an amateur, his photographs won a local prize.

teenWords.meaning: Clearly visible or understood; obvious.
teenWords.tip: Double P and an -ent ending: a-PP-ar-ent.
teenWords.sentence: It was apparent from her smile that she had passed the exam.

teenWords.root: Latin 'argumentum' (proof, evidence) from arguere (to make clear)
teenWords.meaning: A reasoned case for or against something; also a verbal disagreement.
teenWords.tip: Drop the E of 'argue' before -ment: argu + ment.
teenWords.sentence: His argument convinced the judges to change their decision.

teenWords.root: Greek 'arithmetike' (the art of counting) from arithmos (number)
teenWords.meaning: The branch of mathematics dealing with basic number operations.
teenWords.tip: Mnemonic: 'A Rat In The House May Eat The Ice Cream'.
teenWords.sentence: Young children learn arithmetic before moving on to algebra.

teenWords.root: Latin 'assessus' from assidere (to sit beside a judge)
teenWords.meaning: The evaluation or judgment of something's quality or value.
teenWords.tip: Double S twice: a-SS-e-SS-ment.
teenWords.sentence: The final assessment will count for half of your grade.

teenWords.meaning: The murder of an important person, usually for political reasons.
teenWords.tip: Two double-S pairs with two double-S men inside: a-SS-a-SS-in.
teenWords.sentence: The assassination of the archduke helped trigger the First World War.

teenWords.meaning: In the most important or fundamental respects.
teenWords.tip: Basic + ally: keep both parts intact — basic-ally.
teenWords.sentence: Basically, the plan is to save money by cooking at home.

teenWords.meaning: The start or first part of something.
teenWords.tip: Double N: begin + ning — the N doubles just like in 'running'.
teenWords.sentence: At the beginning of the film, the hero is still a child.

teenWords.meaning: To accept something as true.
teenWords.tip: I before E after L: be-LIE-ve — and it hides the word 'lie'.
teenWords.sentence: I believe the library opens at nine on Saturdays.

teenWords.root: Latin 'beneficium' (a kindness) from bene (well) + facere (to do)
teenWords.meaning: Producing good results; helpful.
teenWords.tip: One F, and a -cial ending like 'special': benefi-cial.
teenWords.sentence: Regular exercise is beneficial to both body and mind.

teenWords.meaning: A line that marks the limits of an area.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ary, and keep the A after 'bound': bound-A-ry.
teenWords.sentence: The river forms a natural boundary between the two farms.

teenWords.root: Latin 'calendarium' (account book) from calendae (the first day of the month)
teenWords.meaning: A system or chart for organizing the days, weeks, and months of the year.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ar, not -er: calend-AR.
teenWords.sentence: She circled the exam date on her calendar.

teenWords.root: Greek 'kategoria' (an accusation; a class in logic)
teenWords.meaning: A class or group of things with shared characteristics.
teenWords.tip: Cat + e + gory: the E in the middle is quiet but written.
teenWords.sentence: Each book in the contest belongs to a single category.

teenWords.meaning: A place where dead people are buried.
teenWords.tip: All E's and no A's: c-E-m-E-t-E-ry.
teenWords.sentence: The old cemetery sits on a hill above the village.

teenWords.root: Old French 'changier' from Latin cambiare (to exchange)
teenWords.meaning: Able to change or be changed; unpredictable.
teenWords.tip: Keep the E of 'change' so the G stays soft: change-able.
teenWords.sentence: Spring weather in the mountains is famously changeable.

teenWords.root: French 'collegue' from Latin collega (a partner in office)
teenWords.meaning: A person one works with.
teenWords.tip: Double L and a silent -ue ending: colleag-UE.
teenWords.sentence: My colleague covered my classes while I was ill.

teenWords.meaning: A tall vertical pillar; also a vertical arrangement of items.
teenWords.tip: Silent N at the end: colum-N, like 'autumn' and 'condemn'.
teenWords.sentence: The marble column supports the roof of the temple.

teenWords.meaning: Dedicated to a cause; also, having carried out an act.
teenWords.tip: Double M and double T: co-MM-i-TT-ed.
teenWords.sentence: She is deeply committed to protecting the local wetlands.

teenWords.meaning: A group of people chosen to do a particular job or make decisions.
teenWords.tip: Double M, double T, double E: commi-TT-EE.
teenWords.sentence: The committee meets every Tuesday to plan the festival.

teenWords.meaning: In every way; totally.
teenWords.tip: Complete + ly: keep the final E of 'complete'.
teenWords.sentence: The instructions were completely different from what we expected.

teenWords.meaning: To express strong disapproval of; to sentence a person.
teenWords.tip: Silent N at the end: condem-N, like 'column' and 'autumn'.
teenWords.sentence: The mayor was quick to condemn the vandalism.

teenWords.meaning: General agreement among a group.
teenWords.tip: Con + sensus: it is built on 'sense', with a single S in the middle.
teenWords.sentence: After hours of debate, the council reached a consensus.

teenWords.meaning: Public disagreement or heated debate about something.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -sy, not -cy: controver-SY.
teenWords.sentence: The new highway plan caused great controversy in the town.

teenWords.meaning: To exchange letters; also, to match or be equivalent to.
teenWords.tip: Double R: co-RR-espond — think of 'respond' with 'cor-' in front.
teenWords.sentence: The witnesses' stories correspond in almost every detail.

teenWords.meaning: A strong desire to learn or know something.
teenWords.tip: Drop the U of 'curious' and add -ity: curios-ity.
teenWords.sentence: Her curiosity about insects led her to study biology.

teenWords.root: Latin 'decipere' (to catch, cheat) from de- + capere (to take)
teenWords.meaning: To mislead someone into believing something false.
teenWords.tip: E before I after C: de-CEI-ve — the famous 'except after C' case.
teenWords.sentence: The magician's tricks deceive the eye but not the camera.

teenWords.root: Latin 'desperatus' (given up hope) from de- + sperare (to hope)
teenWords.meaning: Feeling or showing a hopeless sense of urgency.
teenWords.tip: It ends in -ate and is not spelled like 'separate': DES-perate.
teenWords.sentence: The thirsty hikers were desperate for water.

teenWords.meaning: A way in which people or things are not the same.
teenWords.tip: Double F, and it ends in -ence: di-FF-er-ence.
teenWords.sentence: The main difference between the twins is their handwriting.

teenWords.root: Greek 'dilemma' (double proposition) from di- (twice) + lemma (a premise)
teenWords.meaning: A difficult choice between two undesirable options.
teenWords.tip: One L, then double M: di-le-MM-a.
teenWords.sentence: She faced a dilemma: accept the job abroad or stay near her family.

teenWords.meaning: To fail to fulfill someone's hopes or expectations.
teenWords.tip: One S in the prefix but double P: dis-a-PP-oint.
teenWords.sentence: I hope the low turnout will not disappoint the performers.

teenWords.meaning: Causing great damage or destruction.
teenWords.tip: No E after the T: disastr-ous, even though 'disaster' ends in -er.
teenWords.sentence: The flood had a disastrous effect on the harvest.

teenWords.meaning: Training to act according to rules; also a field of study.
teenWords.tip: Remember the SC in the middle: di-SC-ipline.
teenWords.sentence: Daily discipline is what turns practice into mastery.

teenWords.meaning: A long period with little or no rain.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ought like 'brought', and the GH is silent: dr-OUGHT.
teenWords.sentence: The drought left the reservoir at its lowest level in decades.

teenWords.meaning: Constituting number eight in a series.
teenWords.tip: Eight + h: only one T stands before the H — eigh-TH.
teenWords.sentence: She finished in eighth place in the regional spelling bee.

teenWords.meaning: Having the right to do or obtain something; suitable.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ible, not -able: elig-IBLE.
teenWords.sentence: Only students over twelve are eligible for the advanced class.

teenWords.root: Old French 'environnement' (a surrounding) from virer (to turn)
teenWords.meaning: The natural world around us; also, one's surroundings.
teenWords.tip: Do not drop the N before -ment: enviro-N-ment.
teenWords.sentence: Planting trees is one way to protect the environment.

teenWords.root: Old French 'esquiper' (to fit out a ship)
teenWords.meaning: The tools and items needed for a particular activity.
teenWords.tip: One P and no trailing E: equip + ment.
teenWords.sentence: The laboratory equipment must be cleaned after every experiment.

teenWords.meaning: More than usual; particularly.
teenWords.tip: Especial + ly: keep the -ial before the -ly.
teenWords.sentence: The soup tastes especially good on cold winter evenings.

teenWords.meaning: Extremely good; outstanding.
teenWords.tip: Double L and an -ent ending: exce-LL-ent.
teenWords.sentence: She gave an excellent presentation on ocean currents.

teenWords.root: Latin 'existentia' from exsistere (to come into being)
teenWords.meaning: The state or fact of being real or living.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ence, and there is an I after the X: ex-I-stence.
teenWords.sentence: Scientists still debate the existence of life on other planets.

teenWords.meaning: Knowledge or skill gained from doing or seeing things.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ence with an I before it: exper-I-ence.
teenWords.sentence: Traveling alone gave him valuable experience.

teenWords.meaning: Well known from long or close association.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ar, not -er: famili-AR — think of 'family' plus -ar.
teenWords.sentence: The song sounded familiar, though I could not name it.

teenWords.root: Latin 'Februarius' (the month of purification rituals, februa)
teenWords.meaning: The second month of the year.
teenWords.tip: The first R is easy to skip: Feb-RU-ary — say it slowly.
teenWords.sentence: February is the shortest month of the year.

teenWords.meaning: From or relating to a country other than one's own.
teenWords.tip: The G is silent and the order is -eign: for-EIGN, like 'reign'.
teenWords.sentence: Learning a foreign language opens a window onto another culture.

teenWords.meaning: The number 40.
teenWords.tip: No U: it is 'forty', not 'fourty' — the only 'four' word that drops the U.
teenWords.sentence: Forty students signed up for the science fair.

teenWords.meaning: To achieve or carry out something promised or required.
teenWords.tip: Two L's at the start and the end, one in the middle: ful-fill (US spelling).
teenWords.sentence: He worked hard to fulfill his promise to his grandmother.

teenWords.meaning: The group of people who rule or manage a country or state.
teenWords.tip: Do not drop the N: gover-N-ment.
teenWords.sentence: The government announced new funding for rural schools.

teenWords.meaning: The rules of a language governing how words are combined.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -ar, not -er: gramm-AR.
teenWords.sentence: Good grammar helps your writing sound clear and confident.

teenWords.root: Old French 'garantie' from a Germanic root meaning 'to protect'
teenWords.meaning: A formal promise that something will happen or be done.
teenWords.tip: Starts with GUA- and ends with double E: gua-ran-TEE.
teenWords.sentence: The watch comes with a two-year guarantee.

teenWords.meaning: The state of feeling pleased or content.
teenWords.tip: The Y of 'happy' changes to I: happi-ness.
teenWords.sentence: Her happiness was obvious when she heard the results.

teenWords.meaning: To trouble or annoy someone repeatedly.
teenWords.tip: One R, double S: ha-R-a-SS — unlike 'embarrass', which has two R's.
teenWords.sentence: Please do not harass the animals at the zoo.

teenWords.meaning: The measurement of someone or something from bottom to top.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -eight like 'weight': h-EIGHT.
teenWords.sentence: The height of the tower is over three hundred meters.

teenWords.meaning: Causing laughter; amusing.
teenWords.tip: Humor + ous (US spelling drops the U of 'humour').
teenWords.sentence: His humorous stories kept the whole class laughing.

teenWords.meaning: At once; without delay.
teenWords.tip: Double M and an -ately ending: i-MM-ediately.
teenWords.sentence: When the bell rings, leave the building immediately.

teenWords.meaning: The ability to learn, understand, and apply knowledge.
teenWords.tip: Double L in the middle and an -ence ending: inte-LL-igence.
teenWords.sentence: Her intelligence and curiosity made her a natural researcher.

teenWords.meaning: To break the flow of something; to stop someone who is speaking.
teenWords.tip: Double R and an -upt ending like 'erupt': inte-RR-upt.
teenWords.sentence: Please do not interrupt while the teacher is explaining.

teenWords.root: Latin 'librarium' (a book chest) from liber (a book)
teenWords.meaning: A place or collection where books are kept for reading or borrowing.
teenWords.tip: Do not swallow the middle R: li-BRAR-y.
teenWords.sentence: The public library offers free classes every weekend.

teenWords.meaning: An official permit to do, own, or use something.
teenWords.tip: C then S: li-C-en-S-e (in US English it is both noun and verb).
teenWords.sentence: You need a license to drive a car on public roads.

teenWords.meaning: The electrical flash of light produced during a thunderstorm.
teenWords.tip: No E: 'lightning' is not 'lightening' — it is simply light + ning.
teenWords.sentence: Lightning lit up the sky seconds before the thunder rolled in.

teenWords.meaning: The legal union of two people as partners in life.
teenWords.tip: Double R and an -iage ending: ma-RR-iage.
teenWords.sentence: Their marriage has lasted happily for fifty years.

teenWords.meaning: To get or be given something.
teenWords.tip: E before I after C: re-CEI-ve — the textbook case of the rule.
teenWords.sentence: You will receive your certificate at the ceremony.

teenWords.meaning: Very strange or unusual.
teenWords.tip: A famous rule-breaker: W-EI-rd puts E before I with no C anywhere.
teenWords.sentence: A weird noise came from the attic last night.

teenWords.meaning: To become less intense or widespread.
teenWords.tip: One B: a-bate, not 'abbate'.
teenWords.sentence: After midnight, the storm finally began to abate.

teenWords.meaning: To give up a throne or an important responsibility.
teenWords.tip: Ab- + dicate: the same root as 'dictate' — ab-DIC-ate.
teenWords.sentence: The king chose to abdicate and live quietly in the countryside.

teenWords.root: Latin 'abhorrere' (to shrink back from in horror)
teenWords.meaning: To regard with disgust and hatred.
teenWords.tip: One B, and it ends in -hor like 'horror': ab-HOR.
teenWords.sentence: She abhors cruelty in any form.

teenWords.meaning: Difficult to understand; obscure.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -use, not -uce: abstr-USE — do not confuse it with 'obtuse'.
teenWords.sentence: The professor's abstruse lecture left most students puzzled.

teenWords.meaning: Extremely bad; appalling.
teenWords.tip: One S after the Y, then -mal: abys-MAL, from 'abyss'.
teenWords.sentence: The team's performance in the final was abysmal.

teenWords.root: French 'accolade' (an embrace) from Latin ad- + collum (the neck)
teenWords.meaning: An award or expression of praise.
teenWords.tip: Double C at the start, one L: a-CC-olade.
teenWords.sentence: The young pianist received the festival's highest accolade.

teenWords.meaning: Sharp and critical in tone; also, sour in taste.
teenWords.tip: It ends in -bic: acer-BIC, a close cousin of 'acidic' in spirit.
teenWords.sentence: Her acerbic reviews spared no famous actor.

teenWords.root: Latin 'acumen' (a point, sharpness) from acuere (to sharpen)
teenWords.meaning: The ability to make good judgments quickly and keenly.
teenWords.tip: Acu- as in 'acute': business acumen starts with ACU-.
teenWords.sentence: His financial acumen turned a small shop into a chain.

teenWords.root: Greek 'adamas' (unconquerable; the hardest metal or stone)
teenWords.meaning: Refusing to be persuaded; unyielding.
teenWords.tip: Adam + ant: it ends in -ant, not -ent.
teenWords.sentence: She was adamant that the report be finished by Friday.

teenWords.meaning: Very skilled or proficient at something.
teenWords.tip: Do not confuse with 'adapt': ad-EPT means skilled.
teenWords.sentence: He is adept at solving puzzles under pressure.

teenWords.meaning: Excessive admiration or flattery.
teenWords.tip: Adul- like 'adult' minus the T, plus -ation.
teenWords.sentence: The actor grew weary of the public's constant adulation.

teenWords.meaning: Concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty.
teenWords.tip: Starts with the AE digraph: aes-thetic — that AE is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: The architect cared as much about aesthetic appeal as about strength.

teenWords.root: Latin 'affabilis' (easy to speak to) from fari (to speak)
teenWords.meaning: Friendly and easy to talk to.
teenWords.tip: Double F and an -able ending: a-FF-able.
teenWords.sentence: The affable guide made every visitor feel welcome.

teenWords.meaning: Wealthy; having a great deal of money.
teenWords.tip: Double F and an -ent ending: a-FF-lu-ent.
teenWords.sentence: They moved to an affluent suburb with excellent schools.

teenWords.meaning: To make suffering or a problem less severe.
teenWords.tip: Double L and an -iate ending: a-LL-eviate.
teenWords.sentence: The new bridge should alleviate traffic in the town center.

teenWords.meaning: Showing unselfish concern for the welfare of others.
teenWords.tip: Altr- comes from 'alter' (other): altru-istic.
teenWords.sentence: Her altruistic work at the food bank inspired her classmates.

teenWords.meaning: Open to more than one interpretation; unclear.
teenWords.tip: Ambi- (both) plus -guous: the U after the G is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: His ambiguous answer could have meant either yes or no.

teenWords.root: German 'Ambivalenz' from Latin ambi- (both) + valere (to be strong)
teenWords.meaning: Having mixed feelings about something.
teenWords.tip: Ambi- + valent: it ends in -alent, like 'equivalent'.
teenWords.sentence: She felt ambivalent about moving to a new city.

teenWords.meaning: Friendly and without disagreement.
teenWords.tip: Ami- as in 'amiable', plus -cable: ami-CABLE.
teenWords.sentence: The two neighbors reached an amicable agreement about the fence.

teenWords.root: Greek 'anarkhia' (without a ruler) from an- + arkhos (chief)
teenWords.meaning: A state of disorder due to the absence of government or control.
teenWords.tip: The CH is pronounced K, from Greek 'arkhos': anar-CHY.
teenWords.sentence: When the power grid failed, the port city nearly fell into anarchy.

teenWords.meaning: Severe mental or physical suffering.
teenWords.tip: Ang- + uish: the GUI in the middle is the tricky part.
teenWords.sentence: He was in anguish over the loss of his childhood home.

teenWords.meaning: Strong hostility or dislike.
teenWords.tip: Anim- as in 'animal' plus -osity: animos-ity.
teenWords.sentence: Old animosity between the rival schools faded over time.

teenWords.meaning: Something that deviates from what is normal or expected.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -aly, not -oly: anom-ALY.
teenWords.sentence: The warm winter day was an anomaly in the region's climate records.

teenWords.meaning: A thing that existed before or logically precedes another.
teenWords.tip: Ante- (before) + cedent: ante-CED-ent.
teenWords.sentence: Every revolution has antecedents in earlier unrest.

teenWords.meaning: A person or thing that is the direct opposite of another.
teenWords.tip: Anti- + thesis: the second T belongs to 'thesis'.
teenWords.sentence: Her quiet lifestyle is the antithesis of her brother's glamorous one.

teenWords.meaning: Lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern.
teenWords.tip: A- + pathy, from 'pathos' (feeling): a-PATH-y.
teenWords.sentence: Voter apathy worried the election officials.

teenWords.meaning: The highest point of something.
teenWords.tip: Short and sharp: A-P-E-X — resist adding an extra P.
teenWords.sentence: At the apex of her career, she won three awards in one year.

teenWords.meaning: Anxious or fearful that something bad will happen.
teenWords.tip: Double P and an -ensive ending: a-PP-rehensive.
teenWords.sentence: He felt apprehensive before his first driving test.

teenWords.root: Latin 'arbitrarius' (depending on the will of a judge)
teenWords.meaning: Based on random choice rather than on reason or system.
teenWords.tip: The second R is often dropped in speech: arbi-TRAR-y keeps both.
teenWords.sentence: The arbitrary deadline frustrated the research team.

teenWords.meaning: Very old or old-fashioned; no longer in common use.
teenWords.tip: The CH is pronounced K, and it ends in -aic: ar-CHA-ic.
teenWords.sentence: The manuscript uses archaic spellings such as 'hath'.

teenWords.meaning: Requiring great effort; strenuous.
teenWords.tip: Ard- + uous: the UO ending is unusual — ard-UO-us.
teenWords.sentence: Climbing the north face was an arduous journey of six days.

teenWords.meaning: Able to express ideas clearly; also, to pronounce distinctly.
teenWords.tip: Articul- + ate: the CUL in the middle is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: She is an articulate speaker who keeps audiences engaged.

teenWords.meaning: Practicing severe self-discipline and avoiding all indulgence.
teenWords.tip: One S at the start and the C sounds like S: a-SCE-tic.
teenWords.sentence: The ascetic monk owned nothing but a robe and a wooden bowl.

teenWords.root: Latin 'assiduus' (sitting down to a task, constant)
teenWords.meaning: Showing great care, attention, and perseverance.
teenWords.tip: Double S and a -uous ending: a-SS-id-UO-us.
teenWords.sentence: Assiduous revision turned his weakest subject into his strongest.

teenWords.meaning: Having sharp judgment; shrewd and perceptive.
teenWords.tip: Ast- + ute: it ends with a silent E — do not confuse it with 'astound'.
teenWords.sentence: An astute investor, she sold her shares before the market fell.

teenWords.root: Greek 'atrophia' (lack of nourishment) from a- + trophe (food)
teenWords.meaning: The wasting away of a body part or tissue; also, gradual decline.
teenWords.tip: A- + trophy — it literally ends with the word 'trophy'.
teenWords.sentence: Muscles atrophy quickly when a limb is kept in a cast.

teenWords.meaning: Bold, daring, and unrestrained.
teenWords.tip: Auda- + cious: the ending echoes 'spacious'.
teenWords.sentence: Her audacious plan to sail solo across the Atlantic amazed everyone.

teenWords.meaning: To make something greater in size, number, or amount.
teenWords.tip: Aug- as in 'August': aug-MENT, with AU at the start.
teenWords.sentence: He took a weekend job to augment his savings.

teenWords.root: Latin 'auspicium' (divination from the flight of birds)
teenWords.meaning: Conducive to success; favorable.
teenWords.tip: It looks like 'suspicious' with the first S swapped for an A: au-SPICIOUS.
teenWords.sentence: The sunny morning was an auspicious start to the voyage.

teenWords.meaning: Severe or strict in manner or attitude; without decoration.
teenWords.tip: Au- + stere: it ends in -ere, not -ear.
teenWords.sentence: The courtroom had an austere, formal atmosphere.

teenWords.meaning: The right or condition of self-government; independence.
teenWords.tip: Auto- (self) + nomy (law): auto-NOMY.
teenWords.sentence: The region was granted autonomy after decades of campaigning.

teenWords.meaning: A strong dislike or disinclination.
teenWords.tip: Aver- + sion: one S in the -sion ending.
teenWords.sentence: He has a strong aversion to public speaking.

teenWords.root: French 'banal' (common, trite), originally 'belonging to the feudal ban'
teenWords.meaning: So lacking in originality as to be boring.
teenWords.tip: One N: ba-NAL — and it is pronounced buh-NAHL.
teenWords.sentence: The film's banal plot put half the audience to sleep.

teenWords.meaning: To surround with troops; to beset with difficulties.
teenWords.tip: Be- + leaguer, as in 'league': the EA is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: Reporters continued to beleaguer the minister with questions.

teenWords.root: From 'muse' (to ponder) with the prefix be-
teenWords.meaning: Puzzled, confused, or bewildered.
teenWords.tip: Be- + mused: bemused means puzzled, not amused.
teenWords.sentence: The bemused tourists stared at the untranslated sign.

teenWords.meaning: Gentle and kind; in medicine, not harmful or dangerous.
teenWords.tip: The G is silent: be-NIGN, like 'sign' with an N inside.
teenWords.sentence: Fortunately, the biopsy showed that the tumor was benign.

teenWords.root: From 'rate' (to scold) with the prefix be-
teenWords.meaning: To scold or criticize angrily.
teenWords.tip: Be- + rate: one R and one T, rhyming with 'narrate'.
teenWords.sentence: The coach did not berate the players after their narrow loss.

teenWords.root: Old English 'bereafod', past participle of bereave (to deprive)
teenWords.meaning: Deprived of or lacking something; lonely and sad after a loss.
teenWords.tip: Be- + reft: it ends in -eft and is the old past form of 'bereave'.
teenWords.sentence: After the factory closed, the town felt bereft of hope.

teenWords.meaning: To support or strengthen; also, a long cushion.
teenWords.tip: Bol- + ster: picture the pillow that props you up.
teenWords.sentence: Good reviews bolstered the young author's confidence.

teenWords.root: From 'bombast' (cotton stuffing for garments), via Old French
teenWords.meaning: High-sounding in language but with little meaning; inflated.
teenWords.tip: It starts with 'bomb': bomb-ASTIC.
teenWords.sentence: His bombastic speech promised everything and explained nothing.

teenWords.meaning: Relating to the pleasant aspects of life in the countryside.
teenWords.tip: Bu- + colic: the U right after the B is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: The poem paints a bucolic scene of shepherds and green hills.

teenWords.meaning: To grow or increase rapidly; to flourish.
teenWords.tip: It ends in -eon, a cousin of 'pigeon': burg-EON.
teenWords.sentence: New cafes began to burgeon along the renovated waterfront.

teenWords.meaning: The quality of being open and honest in expression.
teenWords.tip: US spelling ends in -or, not -our: cand-OR.
teenWords.sentence: I appreciated her candor about the project's problems.

teenWords.root: Latin 'capitulare' (to draw up under headings) from capitulum (a chapter)
teenWords.meaning: To cease resisting an opponent; to surrender.
teenWords.tip: Capit- + ulate: picture the word 'chapter' (capitulum) hidden inside.
teenWords.sentence: After a long siege, the garrison had to capitulate.

teenWords.meaning: Able to burn tissue; of remarks, sarcastic and bitter.
teenWords.tip: Cau- as in 'cause': caus-TIC.
teenWords.sentence: Her caustic wit made colleagues nervous at meetings.

teenWords.meaning: To express severe disapproval of; a formal reprimand.
teenWords.tip: Cen- + sure: censure means blame — do not confuse it with 'censor', to ban.
teenWords.sentence: The committee voted to censure the official for misconduct.

teenWords.meaning: Of the brain; intellectual rather than emotional.
teenWords.tip: The middle E is easy to drop: cere-BRAL.
teenWords.sentence: Chess is a cerebral game that rewards patience.

teenWords.meaning: Wary and unwilling to take risks; cautious.
teenWords.tip: Circum- (around) + spect (look): circum-SPECT.
teenWords.sentence: The circumspect diplomat chose every word with care.

teenWords.meaning: A person claiming the power to see future events or things beyond ordinary sight.
teenWords.tip: Clair- (clear in French) + voyant (seeing): the I after the A is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: The fairground clairvoyant predicted a journey across the sea.

teenWords.meaning: Kept secret, often for an illicit purpose.
teenWords.tip: Clan- + destine: it ends like 'destiny' without the Y.
teenWords.sentence: The rebels held clandestine meetings deep in the forest.

teenWords.meaning: To come together and form one mass or whole.
teenWords.tip: Co- + alesce: the A right after CO is easy to miss.
teenWords.sentence: The two movements coalesced into a single political party.

teenWords.root: Latin 'coercere' (to restrain) from co- + arcere (to shut in)
teenWords.meaning: To persuade an unwilling person by force or threats.
teenWords.tip: Co- + erce: the ending sounds like 'fierce' without the I.
teenWords.sentence: No one should be coerced into signing an agreement.

teenWords.meaning: Having knowledge or awareness of something.
teenWords.tip: Cog- as in 'recognize': cogni-ZANT, with a G before the N.
teenWords.sentence: Investors must be cognizant of the risks involved.

teenWords.root: Latin 'collusio' (a playing together; a secret agreement)
teenWords.meaning: Secret cooperation for a deceitful or illegal purpose.
teenWords.tip: Double L and a -usion ending like 'illusion': co-LL-usion.
teenWords.sentence: The two firms were accused of collusion to fix prices.

teenWords.meaning: To honor and preserve the memory of a person or event.
teenWords.tip: Double M, then 'memory' hides inside: co-MM-emorate.
teenWords.sentence: A statue was built to commemorate the town's founders.

teenWords.meaning: Corresponding in size or degree; in proportion.
teenWords.tip: Double M and an -urate ending: co-MM-ensurate.
teenWords.sentence: The punishment was not commensurate with the offense.

teenWords.meaning: Smugly satisfied with oneself, unaware of potential danger.
teenWords.tip: Complac- + ent: not 'complaisant', which means eager to please.
teenWords.sentence: After ten straight wins, the team grew complacent.

teenWords.root: Latin 'concedere' (to yield) from con- + cedere (to go)
teenWords.meaning: To admit that something is true; to surrender a point.
teenWords.tip: Con- + cede, as in 'precede': con-CEDE.
teenWords.sentence: He finally conceded that his opponent's argument was stronger.

teenWords.meaning: Intended to placate or reconcile.
teenWords.tip: Concili- + atory: the second I is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: She offered a conciliatory smile after the argument.

teenWords.meaning: Brief and to the point; giving much information in few words.
teenWords.tip: Con- + cise: it ends like 'precise'.
teenWords.sentence: A concise summary should fit on a single page.

teenWords.root: Latin 'condonare' (to forgive, to give up a claim)
teenWords.meaning: To accept or overlook behavior considered morally wrong.
teenWords.tip: Con- + done: it looks exactly like 'done' with 'con-' in front.
teenWords.sentence: The school does not condone bullying in any form.

teenWords.meaning: A large, destructive, uncontrolled fire.
teenWords.tip: Conflag- + ration: the G after FLA is written even when barely heard.
teenWords.sentence: The warehouse fire grew into a conflagration that lit up the night sky.

teenWords.meaning: To confuse and surprise; to mix up two things.
teenWords.tip: Con- + found: it ends with the ordinary word 'found'.
teenWords.sentence: The magician's final trick served to confound the entire audience.

teenWords.root: Latin 'congenialis' (of the same spirit) from genius (nature)
teenWords.meaning: Pleasant because of shared tastes or qualities; agreeable.
teenWords.tip: Con- + genial (friendly): congeni-AL.
teenWords.sentence: They found congenial companions on the hiking trip.

teenWords.root: Latin 'conjectura' (an inference) from conicere (to throw together)
teenWords.meaning: An opinion formed on incomplete information; a guess.
teenWords.tip: Conject- + ure: the CT buried in the middle is the trap.
teenWords.sentence: Without evidence, his theory remained pure conjecture.

teenWords.root: Latin 'consternatio' (alarm) from consternare (to throw into confusion)
teenWords.meaning: Feelings of anxiety or dismay at something unexpected.
teenWords.tip: Conster- + nation: the word 'nation' sits at the end.
teenWords.sentence: The sudden announcement caused consternation among the staff.

teenWords.meaning: Dependent on something else; also, a group sharing a common aim.
teenWords.tip: Contin- + gent: it ends in -gent, like 'urgent'.
teenWords.sentence: Our picnic plans are contingent on the weather.

teenWords.meaning: Feeling remorseful and penitent.
teenWords.tip: Con- + trite: a single T in the middle — con-TRITE.
teenWords.sentence: The contrite student apologized for breaking the window.

teenWords.root: Origin unknown; first recorded as Oxford University slang in the 1500s
teenWords.meaning: A confusing and difficult problem or question.
teenWords.tip: Co- + nundrum: two N's frame the U — co-NUN-drum.
teenWords.sentence: The engineers faced a conundrum: the bridge had to be both light and strong.

teenWords.meaning: Extremely complex and difficult to follow.
teenWords.tip: Convo- + luted: 'lute' hides at the end — convol-UTED.
teenWords.sentence: The novel's convoluted plot confused many readers.

teenWords.root: Greek 'aigis' (the goatskin shield of Zeus and Athena)
teenWords.meaning: Protection, backing, or sponsorship.
teenWords.tip: AE at the start and a hard G: AE-GIS, pronounced EE-jis.
teenWords.sentence: The charity operates under the aegis of the city council.

teenWords.meaning: Opposition to the withdrawal of state support from an established church.
teenWords.tip: Chunk it: anti-dis-establish-ment-arian-ism — 28 letters, with 'establishment' in the middle.
teenWords.sentence: In history class we learned that antidisestablishmentarianism is famous more for its length than its use.

teenWords.meaning: The loss of a letter or sound from the beginning of a word, as in 'squire' from 'esquire'.
teenWords.tip: The AE digraph again: a-PHAE-resis.
teenWords.sentence: Through aphaeresis, 'esquire' shrank over the centuries into 'squire'.

teenWords.meaning: A musical grace note that 'leans' on the main note, taking part of its time.
teenWords.tip: Double P and double G: a-PP-o-GG-iatura — a leaning Italian note.
teenWords.sentence: The soprano's appoggiatura added a sigh of emotion before the main note.

teenWords.meaning: The act of listening to sounds within the body, usually with a stethoscope.
teenWords.tip: Aus- + cultation: the word 'cult' hides inside it.
teenWords.sentence: Through auscultation, the doctor detected a faint heart murmur.

teenWords.meaning: A thing of little importance; also a light musical piece or a table game with balls and pins.
teenWords.tip: Baga- + telle: one G, and a double L in the French ending.
teenWords.sentence: Compared with the cost of the house, the repair fee was a mere bagatelle.

teenWords.meaning: A free-diving, self-propelled vessel built for deep-sea exploration.
teenWords.tip: Bathy- (deep) + scaphe (boat): the PH sounds like F.
teenWords.sentence: The bathyscaphe Trieste carried two explorers to the bottom of the Mariana Trench.

teenWords.meaning: A lullaby, or a quiet instrumental piece in the style of one.
teenWords.tip: Ber- + ceuse: the CEU cluster is pure French.
teenWords.sentence: Chopin's Berceuse rocks as gently as a cradle song.

teenWords.meaning: A temporary camp without tents or cover, used by soldiers or mountaineers.
teenWords.tip: One V, and it ends in -ouac — no K at the end.
teenWords.sentence: The climbers set up a bivouac on a narrow ledge for the night.

teenWords.root: Named for Louis Antoine de Bougainville, the French explorer
teenWords.meaning: A tropical woody vine known for its brightly colored papery bracts.
teenWords.tip: Bougain- + villea: the '-villea' ending carries a double L.
teenWords.sentence: Pink bougainvillea spilled over the garden wall.

teenWords.root: French, from Provencal 'bolhabaissa' (boil + lower the heat)
teenWords.meaning: A rich Provencal fish stew flavored with herbs and saffron.
teenWords.tip: Bouill- + abaisse: double L, then double S — a festival of French spelling.
teenWords.sentence: In Marseille we tasted bouillabaisse made with five kinds of fish.

teenWords.meaning: Grilled bread rubbed with garlic and topped with tomatoes or other ingredients.
teenWords.tip: Say broo-SKET-ta: the SCH is a hard K sound, and the T doubles.
teenWords.sentence: We started the meal with bruschetta piled high with chopped tomatoes.

teenWords.meaning: A watertight chamber used for underwater construction; also a horse-drawn wagon for ammunition.
teenWords.tip: Cai- + sson: double S, and the AI sounds like 'ay'.
teenWords.sentence: Workers inside the caisson dug the foundations for the bridge pier.

teenWords.meaning: Mutual trust and friendship among people who spend much time together.
teenWords.tip: Ca-ma-ra-de-rie: five syllables, ending in the French -erie.
teenWords.sentence: Years of training together built a deep camaraderie within the team.

teenWords.root: Portuguese, probably from Tupi 'ka'a puera' (cleared forest)
teenWords.meaning: A Brazilian martial art combining dance, acrobatics, and music.
teenWords.tip: Capo- + eira: the OEI sequence is the whole battle.
teenWords.sentence: Capoeira players circle and kick in rhythm to the berimbau.

teenWords.meaning: The use of clever but unsound reasoning, especially in moral questions.
teenWords.tip: Casu- + istry: think 'case' fused with 'ministry' — casu-ISTRY.
teenWords.sentence: His defense was dismissed as casuistry designed to excuse the inexcusable.

teenWords.meaning: Inflammation of the mucous membranes, especially in the nose and throat, causing a runny nose.
teenWords.tip: Ends in -arrh: double R and a silent H — cata-RRH.
teenWords.sentence: Spring catarrh from the pollen left her sneezing all morning.

teenWords.root: Named (via Latin) for Chalcedon, an ancient port near modern Istanbul
teenWords.meaning: A translucent variety of quartz, often milky blue or gray.
teenWords.tip: Chal- + cedony: the first CH is a hard K sound.
teenWords.sentence: The ring was set with a pale blue chalcedony.

teenWords.meaning: A person who accompanies and supervises young people; to act as such a companion.
teenWords.tip: One word with a full -one ending: chaper-ONE — in US spelling the final E belongs.
teenWords.sentence: Two teachers agreed to chaperone the school dance.

teenWords.meaning: Cold cooked meats such as sausages and pates, and the shop that sells them.
teenWords.tip: Char- + cuterie: say shar-KOO-tuh-ree, but write every letter.
teenWords.sentence: The charcuterie board held salami, prosciutto, and tiny pickles.

teenWords.root: French 'charivari', probably imitative of the noise
teenWords.meaning: A cacophonous mock serenade for newlyweds, made with pots and horns; a hubbub.
teenWords.tip: Chari- + vari: the CH sounds like SH.
teenWords.sentence: The villagers greeted the wedding with a joyful charivari of clanging lids.

teenWords.root: Named for the Mexican state of Chihuahua
teenWords.meaning: A very small breed of dog with large ears and prominent eyes.
teenWords.tip: Chi- + hua + hua: the HUA repeats — chi-HUA-HUA.
teenWords.sentence: The tiny chihuahua trembled in its owner's arms.

teenWords.meaning: The green pigment in plants that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
teenWords.tip: Chloro- + phyll: PH for the F sound, a Y in the middle, double L at the end.
teenWords.sentence: Chlorophyll is what gives leaves their green color.

teenWords.root: Greek 'Kimmerioi', a mythical people said to live in perpetual darkness
teenWords.meaning: Very dark or gloomy (literary use); also, relating to the mythical Cimmerians.
teenWords.tip: Ci- + mmerian: the double M hides in the middle.
teenWords.sentence: A Cimmerian fog swallowed the harbor before dawn.

teenWords.meaning: An aquatic animal of the phylum Cnidaria, such as a jellyfish, coral, or sea anemone.
teenWords.tip: The C is silent: the word begins CN- — it is spelled like it stings.
teenWords.sentence: A jellyfish is a cnidarian armed with stinging cells.

teenWords.root: Spanish 'cochinilla' (a little insect; also its name in Latin form)
teenWords.meaning: A scarlet dye made from the crushed bodies of a scale insect; also the insect itself.
teenWords.tip: Co- + chineal: the CH sounds like K — cochi-NEAL.
teenWords.sentence: Cochineal gave the cardinals' robes their brilliant red.

teenWords.meaning: A large lobe-finned fish once thought extinct, rediscovered alive in 1938.
teenWords.tip: Coe- + lacanth: the OE pair opens it, and '-canth' (spine) closes it.
teenWords.sentence: The coelacanth is often called a living fossil.

teenWords.root: French 'colporteur' (a peddler), reshaped from col (neck) + porter (to carry)
teenWords.meaning: A person who travels about selling or distributing religious books.
teenWords.tip: Col- + porteur: the French -eur marks 'one who does'.
teenWords.sentence: The colporteur walked the valley with a battered case of Bibles.

teenWords.meaning: A form of Italian comic theater with stock characters and improvised dialogue.
teenWords.tip: Double M: co-MM-edia, as in 'commedia dell'arte'.
teenWords.sentence: In commedia, the clever servant always outwits his master.

teenWords.meaning: A person in a hotel or apartment building who assists guests or residents.
teenWords.tip: Con- + cierge: the CIER in the middle is the maze.
teenWords.sentence: The hotel concierge booked us a table at a tiny bistro.

teenWords.meaning: An adviser, especially to the leader of a crime organization.
teenWords.tip: Consi- + gliere: the Italian GLI is soft in speech but fully written.
teenWords.sentence: In the novel, the consigliere quietly settles every dispute.

teenWords.root: French 'coryphee' from Greek 'koryphaios' (the leader of the chorus)
teenWords.meaning: A leading dancer in a ballet company, ranking just below the soloists.
teenWords.tip: Cory- + phee: the PH sounds like F and the word ends in -EE.
teenWords.sentence: After three seasons she was promoted to coryphee.

teenWords.meaning: In British English, a zucchini; a small summer squash.
teenWords.tip: Cour- + gette: double T and a French -ette ending.
teenWords.sentence: Slice the courgette thinly and grill it with olive oil.

teenWords.meaning: A Hungarian folk dance in two movements, beginning slow and ending in a frenzy.
teenWords.tip: It starts with CZ and there is no H after the C.
teenWords.sentence: The violinist launched into a fiery czardas.

teenWords.root: Named for Anders Dahl, the Swedish botanist
teenWords.meaning: A showy garden flower with tuberous roots, native to Mexico.
teenWords.tip: Dahl + ia: the H belongs to Mr. Dahl — DAHL-ia.
teenWords.sentence: Her dahlias won first prize at the county fair.

teenWords.meaning: A diplomatic step or maneuver, especially a formal representation made to a foreign government.
teenWords.tip: De- + marche ('a walk, a step' in French): it ends with an E.
teenWords.sentence: The ambassador's demarche signaled a sudden shift in policy.

teenWords.meaning: A being responsible for creating the material world, in Platonic and Gnostic thought.
teenWords.tip: Demi- + urge: think 'demi-god' fused with 'urge'.
teenWords.sentence: In Gnostic texts, the demiurge fashions a flawed material world.

teenWords.meaning: A mosquito-borne viral disease causing high fever and severe joint pain.
teenWords.tip: Den- + gue: the final GUE behaves like the end of 'league' minus the A.
teenWords.sentence: Travelers were warned about dengue during the rainy season.

teenWords.meaning: The buttocks, referred to euphemistically.
teenWords.tip: Derr- + iere: double R and the French -iere ending.
teenWords.sentence: The toddler landed squarely on his derriere and laughed.

teenWords.meaning: The state of being only partly or carelessly dressed.
teenWords.tip: Des- + habille: the French word for clothes, 'habits', hides inside.
teenWords.sentence: The portrait shows the duchess in elegant deshabille.

teenWords.meaning: A thick, flat-woven cotton rug made in India.
teenWords.tip: Dhu- + rrie: it starts with DH and doubles the R.
teenWords.sentence: A striped dhurrie covered the wooden floor of the studio.

teenWords.meaning: A mark of two dots placed over a vowel to show it is pronounced separately, as in 'naive' with a trema.
teenWords.tip: Die- + resis: also spelled 'diaeresis' — the E right after the I is the pivot.
teenWords.sentence: One famous magazine still prints the dieresis in 'cooperate' out of tradition.

teenWords.root: Italian 'dilettante' (a lover of the arts) from dilettare (to delight)
teenWords.meaning: A person who cultivates an interest in an art or subject without serious knowledge.
teenWords.tip: Di- + lettante: the double T guards the middle — dile-TT-ante.
teenWords.sentence: He was no dilettante; he had studied ceramics seriously for a decade.

teenWords.root: Arabic 'jallaba', via North African French usage
teenWords.meaning: A long, loose North African robe with full sleeves and a hood.
teenWords.tip: It starts with a silent D: DJ-ellaba, with a double L.
teenWords.sentence: The merchant wore a striped djellaba against the evening chill.

teenWords.meaning: Seeking to apply a doctrine in all circumstances, regardless of practical consequences.
teenWords.tip: Doctrin- + aire: the French -aire ending marks the theorist.
teenWords.sentence: The committee found his doctrinaire approach impossible to bend.

teenWords.meaning: The former basic unit of money in Greece, replaced by the euro.
teenWords.tip: Dra- + chma: the CH is hard, and the word ends in -ma.
teenWords.sentence: Before the euro arrived, Greek prices were quoted in drachma.

teenWords.meaning: A small Alpine plant with woolly, star-shaped white flower heads.
teenWords.tip: Edel- + weiss: WEISS is German for white, and the end is a double S.
teenWords.sentence: Edelweiss grows high on rocky Alpine slopes.

teenWords.meaning: A genus of shrubs and small trees that includes the spindle tree.
teenWords.tip: Four vowels crowd the opening: EUO-nymus.
teenWords.sentence: The euonymus hedge turned scarlet in autumn.

teenWords.meaning: A system of expressing music through bodily movement, developed by Emile Jaques-Dalcroze.
teenWords.tip: Eu- + rythmics: it borrows the YTHM heart of 'rhythm'.
teenWords.sentence: Children in the eurythmics class step and clap the beat of the piano.

teenWords.meaning: A sheet of connective tissue beneath the skin; also a flat horizontal band on a building.
teenWords.tip: Fa- + scia: the SCI sounds like SH — fa-SCIA.
teenWords.sentence: The surgeon carefully repaired the torn fascia.

teenWords.root: Latin roots flocci, nauci, nihili, pili — all mean 'of little or no value'
teenWords.meaning: The action of regarding something as worthless; one of the longest words in English.
teenWords.tip: Build it from four Latin 'worthless' roots: flocci-nauci-nihili-pili-fication — 29 letters.
teenWords.sentence: The professor joked that floccinaucinihilipilification was a useless word, except for spelling it.

teenWords.meaning: A warm, dry wind that blows down the sheltered side of a mountain range, especially the Alps.
teenWords.tip: Foe- + hn: the OE pair does the work at the start.
teenWords.sentence: The foehn melted the spring snow with surprising speed.

teenWords.root: Named for Leonhart Fuchs, the German botanist
teenWords.meaning: A shrub with drooping pinkish-purple flowers; also the vivid purplish-red color itself.
teenWords.tip: Fuchs + ia: the CHS order is the trap — it is Dr. Fuchs's name.
teenWords.sentence: She wore a scarf of vivid fuchsia silk.

teenWords.meaning: A simultaneous discharge of firearms; a rapid outburst of anything.
teenWords.tip: Fusill- + ade: double L, and it begins with the French word for a gun.
teenWords.sentence: A fusillade of questions greeted the celebrity at the airport.

teenWords.meaning: A confused jumble or medley of things.
teenWords.tip: Galli- + maufry: double L, and the '-fry' at the end is a red herring.
teenWords.sentence: The attic was a gallimaufry of toys, ledgers, and broken clocks.

teenWords.meaning: Said as a wish for good health, especially to someone who has just sneezed.
teenWords.tip: Ge- + sundheit: it is literally 'good health' in German.
teenWords.sentence: 'Gesundheit!' she called out after his third enormous sneeze.

teenWords.meaning: Small Italian dumplings made of potato, flour, or semolina.
teenWords.tip: Gno- + cchi: a silent G, then double C with an H — GNOCCHI.
teenWords.sentence: The gnocchi were served in a sage butter sauce.

teenWords.meaning: A nutrient-rich sediment of partly decomposed organic matter found on the beds of certain lakes.
teenWords.tip: Pure Scandinavian squeeze: G-Y-T-T-J-A — two T's, and the J sounds like Y (roughly 'YIT-yuh').
teenWords.sentence: Cores of gyttja revealed centuries of pollen history to the researchers.

teenWords.meaning: A violent dust storm or sandstorm, especially in arid regions.
teenWords.tip: Ha- + boob: the double O sits in the middle like a gust of wind.
teenWords.sentence: A towering haboob swallowed the highway in brown darkness.

teenWords.meaning: A large African antelope with a long face and a sloping back.
teenWords.tip: Harte- + beest: the 'beast' at the end doubles its E.
teenWords.sentence: A lone hartebeest grazed warily near the waterhole.

teenWords.meaning: A crested South American bird whose chicks bear claws on their wings.
teenWords.tip: Hoa- + tzin: the TZ in the middle comes straight from Nahuatl.
teenWords.sentence: The hoatzin is sometimes nicknamed the stinkbird for its manure-like odor.

teenWords.meaning: A flat-heeled Mexican sandal with a woven leather upper; also a thick, filled cornmeal cake.
teenWords.tip: Hua- + rache: the UA opening and the final CHE do the work.
teenWords.sentence: She bought handmade huaraches at the Oaxaca market.

teenWords.meaning: A person's female lover; a woman in love.
teenWords.tip: In- + amor (love) + ata: US spelling uses a single N — inamor-ATA.
teenWords.sentence: In the opera, the count schemes to win back his inamorata.

teenWords.meaning: A narrow strip of land with sea on either side, joining two larger land areas.
teenWords.tip: Isth- + mus: the THM cluster is the crux of the word.
teenWords.sentence: The Panama Canal cuts through the Isthmus of Panama.

teenWords.root: From 'Jagannath' (Puri, India), where the cloth was first made for export
teenWords.meaning: A lightweight cotton cloth used for dresses and linings.
teenWords.tip: Jaco- + net: it sounds like a person's name, but it is named for a city.
teenWords.sentence: The summer frock was sewn from printed jaconet.

teenWords.root: French 'jardiniere' (a female gardener), from jardin (a garden)
teenWords.meaning: An ornamental stand or pot for growing plants; also a garnish of mixed vegetables.
teenWords.tip: Jardin- (garden) + iere: another French -iere ending.
teenWords.sentence: A porcelain jardiniere of ferns stood by the window.

teenWords.meaning: A Dutch breed of sturdy, thick-coated dog with a curled tail and a fox-like face.
teenWords.tip: Kees- + hond: double E first, then the Dutch word for dog.
teenWords.sentence: The keeshond's spectacles and smile charmed the dog-show judges.

teenWords.root: Scots 'carfuffle', from Gaelic car (to twist) + fuffle (disorder)
teenWords.meaning: A commotion or fuss, especially one caused by a disagreement.
teenWords.tip: Ker- + fuffle: a double F fluffs up the middle.
teenWords.sentence: A kerfuffle broke out when the last train was cancelled without notice.

teenWords.root: Reduplication of 'knack' (a trick, a clever device)
teenWords.meaning: A small decorative object of little value.
teenWords.tip: Two silent K's guard this word: KNICK-KNACK.
teenWords.sentence: Every shelf in her room held another porcelain knickknack.

teenWords.meaning: A fruit-eating mammal of Central and South American forests, with a long tail that can grip branches.
teenWords.tip: Kinka- + jou: the JOU ending gives it a French flavor.
teenWords.sentence: The kinkajou reached for the mango, its tail curled firmly around a branch.
